content: 1. Systematic measurements of black carbon (BC) and/or elemental carbon (EC) should be conducted. However, these measurements must not replace or diminish the existing monitoring of pollutants for which guidelines are already established. 2. Efforts should be made to develop emission inventories, conduct exposure assessments, and perform source apportionment studies specifically for black carbon and elemental carbon. 3. Measures should be implemented to reduce emissions of black carbon and elemental carbon within the relevant jurisdiction. Where appropriate, standards or targets for ambient concentrations of BC/EC should be developed. 4. Ambient ultrafine particles (UFPs) should be quantified in terms of particle number concentration (PNC) for a size range with a lower limit of ≤10 nm, without imposing restrictions on the upper size limit. 5. The existing air quality monitoring strategy should be expanded to include UFP monitoring. This should involve size-segregated, real-time PNC measurements at selected air monitoring stations, conducted simultaneously with the monitoring of other airborne pollutants and particulate matter (PM) characteristics. 6. Differentiation between low and high PNC levels is necessary to guide decisions on prioritizing UFP source emission control. Low PNC levels can be defined as <1,000 particles/cm³ (24-hour mean), while high PNC levels can be defined as >10,000 particles/cm³ (24-hour mean) or >20,000 particles/cm³ (1-hour mean). 7. Emerging scientific and technological advancements should be utilized to improve methods for assessing exposure to UFPs. These methods should be applicable to epidemiological studies and UFP management strategies. 8. Air quality management and dust forecasting programs should be maintained. These programs should include early warning systems and short-term air pollution action plans to alert the population to stay indoors and take personal measures to minimize exposure during sand and dust storm (SDS) events with high particulate matter levels. 9. Air quality monitoring programs and reporting procedures should be maintained, including source apportionment activities to quantify and characterize particulate matter composition. This should also determine the percentage contribution of SDS to overall ambient PM concentrations, enabling local authorities to target anthropogenic and natural PM emissions for reduction. 10. Epidemiological studies should be conducted to investigate the long-term health effects of SDS and to enhance understanding of the toxicity of different types of particulate matter. Such studies are particularly recommended in regions where knowledge and data on health risks from frequent SDS exposure are insufficient. 11. Wind erosion control should be implemented through the carefully planned expansion of green spaces, tailored to the specific ecosystem conditions. Regional collaboration among countries affected by SDS is essential to combat desertification and manage green areas effectively. 12. In urban areas with high population density and low rainfall, streets should be cleaned after intense SDS episodes with high dust deposition rates. This short-term measure aims to prevent the resuspension of dust by road traffic. 13. The WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines are a critical tool for policymakers, lawmakers, and technical experts at local, national, and international levels. These guidelines assist in developing and implementing regulations and standards for air quality, pollution control, urban planning, and related policy areas. 14. National and local authorities, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, advocacy groups, and other stakeholders, such as patient organizations, citizen groups, industrial stakeholders, and environmental organizations, are key users of these guidelines. 15. Academics, health and environmental impact assessment practitioners, and researchers in the field of air pollution are also primary users of the guidelines. 16. The guidelines aim to reduce air pollutant levels globally to decrease the significant health burden caused by air pollution exposure. They provide evidence-based recommendations to inform legislation and policy. 17. Compared to previous WHO guidelines, these updated guidelines use new methods for evidence synthesis and guideline development, reinforce existing evidence on the adverse health effects of air pollution, and highlight health risks at lower pollution levels than previously recognized. 18. While achieving the Air Quality Guideline (AQG) levels is the ultimate goal, gradual progress marked by achieving interim targets should be considered a critical indicator of improving population health, especially in regions with high air pollution levels. 19. Implementation of the guidelines requires robust air pollution monitoring systems, public access to air quality data, legally binding and globally harmonized air quality standards, and effective air quality management systems. 20. Policy decisions should prioritize actions based on health risk assessments of air pollution. Collaboration among various sectors and stakeholders is essential, with the health sector playing a crucial role in raising awareness of the health and economic impacts of air pollution and ensuring that health protection is a central focus in policy discussions. 21. Monitoring and evaluation are vital to ensure the effective implementation of the guidelines. Current evidence justifies actions to reduce population exposure to key air pollutants on a global scale, although uncertainties and knowledge gaps remain. 22. Future research will strengthen the scientific evidence base for clean air policy decisions worldwide.
